explanations.answer: Has him beaten and put in the stocks
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Pashhur hears Jeremiah prophesying and has Jeremiah the prophet beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 20:2). Pashhur is the chief official in the house of the LORD, so he's the one who should know better. I think this is a hard one to read, friend.

explanations.answer: Asks him to pray for the whole city
explanations.explanation: I wish it went that way, friend, but it doesn't. Pashhur doesn't ask for prayer at all. The text says he had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:2). A chief official who hears a warning and reaches for the stocks is not a man looking for a prayer partner.

explanations.answer: Brings him before the elders to explain
explanations.explanation: A meeting with the elders sounds so civilized, doesn't it? Pashhur skips the meeting. He has Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 20:2). No explaining, no questions, no sit-down. I think that tells us how he took the message.

explanations.answer: Gives him a new name from the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Jeremiah walks out of those stocks and hands Pashhur a new name: "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib" (Jeremiah 20:3). He doesn't come out whispering, and he doesn't come out quiet. That's a prophet who still has the LORD's word to deliver.

explanations.answer: Thanks him for letting him go free
explanations.explanation: Thank-you note? Nope, friend. Jeremiah doesn't thank Pashhur for anything. He tells him, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib" (Jeremiah 20:3). I think Pashhur was hoping for a quiet exit, and he did not get one.

explanations.answer: Promises to stop prophesying there
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but a night in the stocks didn't shut Jeremiah up. He speaks right to Pashhur and says, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib" (Jeremiah 20:3). He keeps going. He doesn't promise to stop, and he doesn't back up a single step.

explanations.answer: terror
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends" (Jeremiah 20:4). That's what the name Magor-missabib is pointing to. It's a heavy word, so I'll say it plain: it's a hard thing to hear.

explanations.answer: blessing
explanations.explanation: Wish it were a blessing, friend, but no. The LORD says, "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends" (Jeremiah 20:4). A name like Magor-missabib doesn't sound like a blessing, and it isn't one. This word is a hard one.

explanations.answer: warning
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, baker, but that's not the word. The LORD says, "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends" (Jeremiah 20:4). A warning is something you hear. A terror is something that comes upon you. It's heavy, so take it slow.

explanations.answer: Babylon
explanations.explanation: Babylon is right, baker. The LORD says, "I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 20:4). Judah is the land where Pashhur and Jeremiah live. The message was never just about one man in the stocks.

explanations.answer: Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt is a good guess, friend, but the LORD names a different king. He says He will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon, and that king will carry them away to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:4). Same road trip, different destination.

explanations.answer: Assyria
explanations.explanation: Assyria is a name you'd see in other places in the Bible, friend, but not in this one. Here the LORD says, "I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 20:4). Babylon is the word that goes in the blank.

explanations.answer: Enemies will carry it all off
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD says He will give the wealth of this city to their enemies, and they will plunder it, seize it and carry it off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5). That includes all the treasures of the kings of Judah. Nothing on that list gets left behind.

explanations.answer: It will be buried under the temple
explanations.explanation: Hiding the treasure is a clever plan, friend, but it's not the LORD's. He says He will give the wealth of the city to their enemies, who will plunder it and carry it off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5). Nobody is burying anything under the temple.

explanations.answer: It will go to the poor of Judah
explanations.explanation: That would be a very different ending, baker. But the LORD says He will give the city's wealth to their enemies. They will plunder it, seize it and carry it off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5). The poor of Judah aren't mentioned in these verses.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True, baker. The LORD says, "And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house, will go into captivity" (Jeremiah 20:6). Notice that it's his whole house, not just him. The word lands right on his own front door.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's true, friend. The LORD says, "And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house, will go into captivity" (Jeremiah 20:6). That includes everyone in his house, not just him. I think the word hits hard when it comes this close to home.

explanations.answer: He will die and be buried there
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The LORD says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried" (Jeremiah 20:6). It's a sober ending, and the text doesn't soften it. Pashhur goes there and stays there.

explanations.answer: He will rise to serve the king
explanations.explanation: Working for the king of Babylon sounds like a promotion, friend, but that's not in the text. The LORD says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried" (Jeremiah 20:6). Nothing here says Pashhur serves anybody there. This ending is a heavy one.

explanations.answer: He will escape and come home
explanations.explanation: I'd love a happy homecoming, friend, but that's not what the LORD says. He says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried" (Jeremiah 20:6). No escape, no trip home. It's a sad line, and I won't joke about it.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The LORD says Pashhur has been prophesying lies to his friends: "you and all your friends to whom you have prophesied these lies" (Jeremiah 20:6). So the text calls what he said lies, not truth. Jeremiah's message is the one that came from the LORD.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: False is right, baker. The LORD says Pashhur and his friends were the ones "to whom you have prophesied these lies" (Jeremiah 20:6). So what Pashhur told them was lies, not the truth. I think that makes the stocks sit even heavier.
